T. S. Eliot. The American-born poet and critic who became the defining intellectual voice of Anglo-American modernism.

Born in St. Louis, Missouri in 1888 to an old New England family, Eliot felt perpetually displaced, seeking cultural authority in Europe. He studied philosophy at Harvard, then moved to Oxford. There he met and married Vivienne Haigh-Wood in London—a marriage of mutual unhappiness and psychological turbulence that would haunt both their lives. Eliot worked as a banker and then as editor at the Criterion, a journal that became the mouthpiece of modernist aesthetics and his own intellectual vision. In 1927, the same year, he became a British citizen and entered the Anglican Church. This religious conversion marked a decisive turn toward traditionalism and formalism. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1948. His later plays, particularly Murder in the Cathedral, were commercially and critically successful.

His major works include Prufrock and Other Observations, published in 1917. This collection includes "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock," modernism's ur-text of paralysis and indecision. The Waste Land appeared in 1922—433 lines of fragmented, multilingual verse depicting post-World War I spiritual desolation. It draws on myth including Arthurian legend, Dante, and Sanskrit texts. The poem is extensively footnoted. It became a central text of modernism. The Hollow Men, published in 1925, meditates on spiritual emptiness and meaninglessness through haunting, ritualistic language. Four Quartets came out in 1943, four long meditative poems on time, spiritual experience, and the nature of language. It is his most mature and celebrated work.

Eliot's literary philosophy advocates for impersonality in art. The artist should disappear behind the work; emotion should be expressed through objective correlatives—external situations that evoke feeling. He emphasizes difficulty and allusiveness. Great literature draws on the entire European tradition. Readers must be erudite to understand fully. He speaks of a unified sensibility that Romantic poets had dissociated by separating feeling from thought. The metaphysical poets and Elizabethans, he argued, unified them. This becomes a model for modern recovery. He is culturally and religiously conservative, skeptical of democracy, mass culture, and modernism's transgressive impulses despite being modernism's architect.

Eliot's influence on twentieth-century literary culture is almost impossible to overstate. The Waste Land defined how modernism understood itself: fragmented, erudite, alienated, yet rich with cultural memory. His criticism created the canon that universities taught for decades. Yet Eliot's legacy remains deeply contested. His anti-Semitism, his skepticism of democracy, and his dismissal of women writers have made him a figure of ongoing scholarly debate. He represents both modernism's greatest heights and its elitism and conservatism. In quiz bowl, he is the quintessential high modernist: difficult, allusive, personally reserved, spiritually serious.
